newsitem.title: USA: Stocks hit by interest rate fears; Dow off 140 points.
newsitem.headline: Stocks hit by interest rate fears; Dow off 140 points.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks plummeted Thursday as Wall Street was shaken anew by concern over rising interest rates and the prospect of competition from bonds for investment money.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 140.11 points, or 2.04 percent, at 6,740.59 after being off more than 216 in late afternoon. For the week, it was down 64.20 points.

It was the eighth-largest loss in the Dow's history in point terms, but not a top sell-off on a percentage basis. The day's loss brought the Dow about 5 percent below its record closing high of 7,085.16 set on March 11.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,015 to 612 on active volume of 475 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The bear just bit us," said Doug Myers, vice president of equity trading at Interstate/Johnson Lane.
Stocks tracked the slump in bonds, which came after the National Association of Realtors reported stronger-than-expected existing home sales in February.

Existing home sales rose 9 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.26 million, compared with a forecast 4.05 million, the realtors' group said. The January rate was a revised 3.91 million.
The economic report added fuel to the argument that the Federal Reserve will again raise interest rates to cool the economy after it raised a key rate earlier in the week.
On Tuesday, the Fed raised by one quarter-point the federal funds rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.50 percent.
The central bank called the move a "prudent step" to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year. And, it hinted at more action to come.

The key 30-year Treasury bond fell 1-1/4 points, sending its yield up to 7.09 percent -- the higest since mid-September 1996 -- from 6.98 percent at Wednesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Bond yields above 7 percent tend to draw money away from stocks and into bonds.
"Seven percent and a bit of safety is not a bad idea when there's so much uncertainty ahead," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.

Charles White, managing director, Avatar Associates, said "If it becomes more and more apparent as the weeks go by that the economic strength is going to be persistent, then we're looking at more rate hikes and a real challenge for the equity market for the first time in a long time."
Interest-rate sensitive stocks were clipped for the third session in a row following the Fed's rate hike Tuesday.
Citicorp shed 2-5/8 to 111, Wells Fargo & Co. lost 9-1/8 to 292, J.P. Morgan & Co. dropped 2-3/4 to 102-3/4 and Salomon Inc. fell 1-1/8 to 52-1/2.

Quaker Oats Co. conceded defeat in efforts to turn around its struggling Snapple beverage unit and agreed to sell it for $300 million -- $1.4 billion less than it paid for the business -- to Triarc Cos., the owner of rival Mistic beverages. Quaker ended up 1/4 to 37-3/4. Triarc rose 1-5/8 to 17-3/8.

Bre-X Minerals Ltd. plummeted 9-13/32 to 1-31/32 in Nasdaq trading after the Canadian mining company acknowledged that its gold discovery in Indonesia once thought to be the biggest of the century might be far smaller.

Medical device company Medtronic Inc. jumped 4 to 62-3/8 after the company said its pacemaker business was doing well, and the company was aiming for 15 percent compound annual growth in earnings and revenues.
Financial markets will be closed for Good Friday.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 19.57 points to 1,249.51.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 16.62 to 773.88. The American Stock Exchange index was off 5.17 to 577.90.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 7.94 to 407.43. The average share was down 81 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,376.835 down 140.556 or 1.87 percent.
